Questions about how Americans spend their day

What time do most Americans go to bed?

On weeknights, more than half of Americans age 15 and older are asleep by 10:30 PM. Weekends are the same.

What time do most Americans wake up?

On weekdays, fewer than half are still asleep after 6:30 AM. On weekends, people sleep in: the halfway point is 8:00 AM.

How much do Americans sleep?

Americans spend 8 hr 44 min a day asleep on average (8 hr 28 min on weekdays and 9 hr 22 min on weekends), counting naps and excluding time lying awake.

How many Americans are asleep at 3 AM?

About 237.8 million people, or 94.6% of Americans age 15 and older, on an average weekday at 3 AM.

What time do Americans eat lunch and dinner?

Eating peaks at 12:15 PM for lunch (17.1% of people eating) and at 6:15 PM for dinner (14.4%) on weekdays.

When is rush hour?

The share of Americans driving peaks at 7:30 AM in the morning (8.6%) and at 5:00 PM in the afternoon (11.6%, about 29.2 million drivers) on weekdays.

When are the most Americans at work?

On weekdays, work peaks at 10:45 AM, when 40.7% of Americans age 15 and older (about 102.4 million) are working.

How much TV do Americans watch?

Americans age 15 and older spend 2 hr 44 min a day watching TV and movies on average, 2 hr 31 min on weekdays and 3 hr 17 min on weekends.

How many Americans are driving right now?

It depends on the time: at 8 AM on a weekday, about 18.1 million; at 5 PM, about 29.2 million; at 3 AM, about 639,000. American Minute shows the estimate for your local time.

Where do these numbers come from?

From the American Time Use Survey, in which the Census Bureau interviews thousands of Americans each year about everything they did over one day, minute by minute, for the Bureau of Labor Statistics. American Minute pools all 258,954 diaries from 2003 to 2025, weighted to represent the U.S. civilian population age 15 and older. Estimates are for an average day, not a live count.

Can I filter by age, income, race, or state?

Yes. The explorer filters by sex, age, work status, children, race, Hispanic origin, education, earnings, family income, occupation, industry, marital status, region, state, day of the week, month, and more, and by where people were and who they were with.

About these numbers

Estimates come from all 258,954 diaries in the American Time Use Survey (Bureau of Labor Statistics and Census Bureau), 2003–2025, weighted to the U.S. civilian population age 15 and older and pooled across years. Times are local clock time. Counts are people on an average day of that type, not a live count. Weekdays are Monday–Friday. How the estimates work.
